analysis.one_liner: Requires Medicare drug plans to disclose when pharmacy benefit manager committees overrule their own drug-coverage experts.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan Senate bill to force disclosure of pharmacy benefit manager conflicts in Medicare drug formularies was referred to the Finance Committee in July 2023 and never received a hearing or vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill targets a hidden step in how Medicare drug coverage is decided. Medicare drug plans have an expert panel (the pharmacy and therapeutic committee) that recommends which drugs get covered, but the plan or its pharmacy benefit manager can use other internal committees to overrule those experts. The bill would require plans to tell Medicare which committees have that power, list every drug they overruled, explain why, and let the Government Accountability Office study how often this happens and whether it blocks beneficiaries from getting prescribed drugs.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare Part D beneficiaries, who currently cannot see when a plan's own medical experts recommended covering a drug but a committee tied to the plan or its pharmacy benefit manager reversed that decision. Disclosure and a public audit would give Congress and beneficiaries the evidence needed to judge whether these conflicts of interest restrict access to medicines or raise costs.

how_it_helps.text: Plans using formularies must report to Medicare the name, role, and composition of any committee, entity, or individual affiliated with the plan or a contracted pharmacy benefit manager that has authority to make coverage, formulary, or utilization management decisions beyond the standard pharmacy and therapeutic committee [S3].
Plans must list every drug for which such a committee overrode the expert panel's initial recommendation and provide a brief justification for each decision [S3].

The bill also requires the Government Accountability Office to study how prevalent these override committees are, what drugs they touch, and how tools like prior authorization, step therapy, and formulary exclusions affect beneficiary access to drugs, with a report to Congress by January 1, 2029 [S3].
The GAO report and recommendations are aimed at producing future legislative and administrative action [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Pharmacy benefit managers and the Medicare drug plan sponsors that contract with them, who would face new reporting requirements and lose some of the opacity that currently shields their formulary decisions from public view. Indirectly, anyone who benefits from PBM formulary practices if disclosure leads to tighter regulation.
analysis.who_pays_short: PBMs and Medicare drug plan sponsors

drawbacks.text: The bill is disclosure-only: it requires reporting but does not prohibit any practice, cap PBM compensation, or restrict the use of prior authorization, step therapy, or formulary exclusions, so beneficiaries get information without any immediate protection [S3].
The required GAO study and report are not due until January 1, 2029, meaning any evidence produced for further legislation would arrive years after the bill would have taken effect [S3].
Plan sponsors bear new administrative reporting costs each plan year starting in 2026, and the bill waives the Paperwork Reduction Act to impose those requirements without standard review [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The reporting burden on plans and PBMs is modest, and the real limitation is that disclosure by itself changes nothing: a beneficiary denied a drug still gets no remedy. But information is a precondition for fixing the problem. The GAO report was due in 2029, so even a successful bill was designed as a first step toward stronger rules rather than a fix itself.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in July 2023 with bipartisan sponsorship and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, where it sat without a hearing, markup, or floor vote until the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Tom Carper introduced the bill on July 20, 2023, with Sen. Chuck Grassley joining as the cosponsor, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance that same day [S1][S5][S4].
No further action appears in the record: the bill never received a committee hearing, markup, vote, or floor consideration in the 118th Congress [S5].
The bill expired when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, with the entire bill consisting of a reporting requirement and a GAO study [S2][S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pharmacy benefit managers and Medicare drug plan sponsors are better off, because the affiliated-committee practice the bill was meant to expose remains undisclosed, and no evidence base for restricting it was ever produced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Pharmacy benefit managers and drug plan sponsors

for.name: Sen. Tom Carper
for.what_they_did: Introduced the PBM Oversight Act of 2023 in the Senate.

for.name: Sen. Chuck Grassley
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's only cosponsor, giving it bipartisan sponsorship.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee (Chair Ron Wyden)
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill on the day of introduction and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote; the bill died in committee.

against.name: Pharmacy benefit managers
against.role: Industry subject to the disclosure requirements
against.what_they_did: PBM companies and their trade association campaigned broadly against PBM oversight and reform measures during the 118th Congress, in which the major PBMs (CVS Caremark, Express Scripts, Optum Rx) faced bipartisan scrutiny.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan from the start, a Democrat introducing with a single Republican cosponsor, but so few members signed on that the bill never became a partisan fight; it stalled without any recorded votes.

industries.note: The bill would force PBMs' affiliated formulary committees into the open, requiring plans to name them, list every drug they overruled the medical experts on, and justify why. The GAO study would build a public record of how PBM-linked decisions affect beneficiary access to drugs. The bill regulates but does not ban any practice.

industries.industry: Medicare Part D plan sponsors (insurers offering prescription drug plans)
industries.note: Plan sponsors would bear annual reporting costs starting in 2026 and would have to disclose conflicts in their own affiliates as well as their PBMs' committees, but the bill imposes no new restrictions on their conduct.

industries.industry: Consumers of PBM services (Medicare drug plans contracting with PBMs)
industries.note: Plan sponsors would gain visibility into whether their contracted PBMs are steering formularies through hidden committees, information they do not systematically get today, in exchange for their own reporting obligations.
